newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SWIMMING-TIMING GLITCH MARS SWIMMING WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-TIMING GLITCH MARS SWIMMING WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS.

text.p: A malfunctioning timing system brought an Australian protest and red faces from officials on Thursday, the first night of the world short-course swimming championships.

A faulty pressure pad intitially shaved almost two seconds off Australian Michael Klim's time in the men's 100 metres butterfly final and raised doubts about Swede Lars Frolander's 0.04 second win over Australian Geoff Huegill.

"We protested, which as the head coach of a nation we should do," Australian team-leader Don Talbot told reporters after accepting the final times of 51.95 seconds for Frolander, 51.99 for Huegill and 52.02 for third-placed Klim.
"It's not protesting against Frolander, it's protesting against a result that might have been something else because of a malfunction by a piece of machinery," Talbot said.
Peter Heurtzeller, of timing company Omega, said that a pressure pad at the end of Klim's lane, designed to register the touch of a finishing swimmer, was over-sensitive.
"We don't know why, but we will look at it tonight. The waves made the pad react," he told a news conference.
Film from a 100 picture per second video system provided a reliable final time, he added. The pad was changed after the incident and caused no further problems.
"Nearly every meet you go to there's something that happens around timing or judging or changeovers or something. Its not uncommon," Talbot said. "There's no better system unfortunately."
The Australians were able to take comfort from gold medals in both the men's and women's 400 metres individual medley and the men's relay on the opening night of the four-day championships.
